title: TA8-17118
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The first claimant (FC), XXXXX XXXXX (age 29), is a male from the Czech Republic. The second claimant (SC), XXXXX XXXXX (date of birth: XXXXX, 1962, age 48), is a male from the Czech Republic. The third claimant, XXXXX XXXXX (age 29), is a female from the Czech Republic. The fourth claimant, XXXXX XXXXX (age 48), is a female from the Czech Republic. The fifth claimant, XXXXX XXXXX (age 28), is a male from the Czech Republic. The sixth claimant, XXXXX XXXXX (date of birth: XXXXX, 1995, age 14), is a male from the Czech Republic. The seventh claimant, XXXXX XXXXX (date of birth: XXXXX, 2000, age 10), is a male from the Czech Republic. The eighth claimant, XXXXX XXXXX (age 7), is a female from the Czech Republic. The ninth claimant, XXXXX XXXXX (age 4), is a male from the Czech Republic. The FC and the third claimant are common-law spouses of each other. The seventh, eighth claimants and ninth claimants are the children of the FC and the third claimant. The third claimant has been appointed the Designated Representative of her minor children. The SC and the fourth claimant are married to each other. The sixth claimant is the child of the SC and the fourth claimant. The SC has been appointed the Designated Representative of the sixth claimant. The FC and the fifth claimant are children of the fourth claimant. The claimants claim refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

The SC states that he is from the Roma ethnic group and he was not allowed to sit with the non-Roma students at his school. He states there were only two Roma in his class and they were ostracized and made to sit at the very back of the room. They were accused of being filthy and lazy. His classmates would not play with him because of his dark skin. He states that he was treated unfairly and was prevented from participating in after-school programs with the other children. He states that his son, the sixth claimant, was removed from the school soccer team because he was Roma.

He says that when he was 15 years of age some skinhead kids brutally attacked him when he was playing in the snow with some of his friends. He stated that one of the skinhead kids hit him in the groin with a sled and caused severe pain. He says that he was taken to the hospital for emergency surgery and one of his testicles had to be removed.

He maintains that he dropped out of school at age 16 and he obtained work XXXXX XXXXX because that was the only job available to him because of his lack of education. He states that he was persecuted on the job because of his Roma ethnicity. He became self-employed by XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. He says that when he applied for jobs and contracts for this work the job centers would have the letter "R" on a person's card indicating that Roma individuals were not to be considered for job opportunities.

The SC states that his wife, the fourth claimant, suffered several attacks by skinheads. He says on several occasions she was threatened with racial epithets when she was on a bus and she was forced to leave the bus before she reached her destination. He says that sometime in 1995, under the pretext of removing a tumor from her body, the doctors deceitfully removed her womb, making her unable to bear more children. He states that she has not been the same person since then. She suffers from hot flashes, mood swings, some strange painful feelings and depression. He states his wife now has a phobia for medical doctors and is not able to trust them and their services. He states that the incident has affected their married life.

The SC says that his family lived in a mixed neighborhood of Romas and non-Romas. He alleges that in XXXXX 2007, the Caucasian and skinhead residents of the area presented a petition to the non-Roma landlord to cease and desist from renting his apartment to Roma individuals because they were a menace and they defaced the neighborhood.

He says that the fifth claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, is mentally challenged. He states that he was enrolled in a special needs school without the consent of the SC and the fourth claimant. He says that he preformed poorly and repeated grade 1 a couple of times. The teachers were never patient with him. He alleges that he was constantly harassed at school and the teachers would not help him. The SC states that he was attacked in XXXXX 2008, while making a telephone call from a telephone booth in the city of XXXXX. He was taken to hospital and he received four stitches in his head. The SC states that the incident was reported to the police but they have not found any of his attackers.

He states that in 1990, he joined a Roma organization called "KSORN" in an attempt to change the Roma situation socially and politically. He says that each town had a local chapter of this organization and he was responsible for his town's chapter. He states that when he went to Prague for a meeting of this organization he and his friends were attacked. He says that people in his town knew him as a Roma rights activist. He alleges that as a result, he was constantly in danger as his name became well known in the region by the skinheads and he became one of their targets. He alleges that on several occasions, skinheads and even some soldiers attacked members of his organization on their way home after events. He maintains that in XXXXX 2002, he was walking by a public washroom when approximately five soldiers came out of a restaurant and started shouting racial slurs at him, then they attacked him and broke his nose. He states that they also injured his back with a knife. He says that he went to the police report the attack but they took no action despite the fact that they knew the location of the soldiers. He maintains that it took three months to recover from the attack and he still carries the scars.

He states that in 2002, he attended a national congress for the organization in Prague with some other individuals. When they returned and were leaving the train, he and two other individuals by the names of Mr XXXXX and Mr. XXXXX were attacked by skinheads. He alleges that as a result of this attack he lost two front teeth and he had a knife wound on his left foot. He states that the attack was reported to the police but there has never been an arrest. He says that members of the national organization came to XXXXX to obtain an explanation as to how the skinheads knew of their arrival time. He maintains that the Mayor assured them that he would deal with the matter but they never received a report of the investigation. He says that the only feedback they received was that the attackers were probably outsiders. He says that he moved to the village of XXXXX from 2003 to 2005 for protection. However, the attacks continued.
The FC's family then made arrangements to leave the country. They arrived in Canada on September 7, 2008 and they made claims for refugee protection on the same day.

The FC states that his son, the seventh claimant, was put in a special school for disabled and Roma children when he first enrolled in school. He says that he discussed his concerns with the school authorities but they did nothing about the situation. He says that he eventually withdrew his son from the school because he lost interest in attending it.

He says that his wife, the third claimant, had a very difficult childhood. Her mother died when she was very young and she was raised in a foster home. He says that the Caucasian matrons at the home were cruel to her and some other Roma kids in the home. He states that on several occasions they were placed in straight jackets for a lengthy period of time. At other times they were left out in the cold. He alleges that following the birth of the ninth claimant she was given an anesthetic and when she woke up she was told that she could no longer have children because she had been sterilized. He alleges that she was not advised about the sterilization and she was not asked to sign any papers for consent. He maintains that as a result of the sterilization she went into a depression and now relies on pills to be stable. He says that the doctor's actions fell within the statute of limitations and therefore was unpunished. He says that the Czech Council for Human Rights put forth a plan that would compensate victims of forced sterilization but the Czech government claimed that the proposal had little chance of being ratified because of fears that it would set a precedent enabling large numbers of unverifiable claims of medical malpractice.

He states that sometime in XXXXX 2008, he and his wife were on the way to the city of XXXXX to visit family. He states that three skinheads attacked them on the train. He says that he reported the attack to the police but they did not arrest anyone. He says that on another occasion a burning bottle was thrown into his living room window and it exploded inside his home. He maintains that this could have injured any of his children or his wife.

The FC arrived in Canada on September 9, 2008. The members of his family namely, the third, seventh, eighth and nine claimants arrived in Canada on September 7, 2008. They made claims for refugee protection on September 9, 2008.
I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The oral testimony of the FC, the SC, third and fourth claimants and the supporting documentation filed2 establish the claimants' identities as nationals of the Czech Republic. Convention Refugee
The determinative issue is whether the claimants will be persecuted, by reason of their Roma ethnicity, if they return to the Czech Republic.
I find that there is no serious possibility the claimants will be persecuted if they should return to the Czech Republic. Credibility

There were a number of credibility concerns. The SC testified that his wife, the fourth claimant, received a general letter of apology stating that they were not aware of her particular sterilization. The fourth claimant initially testified that she did not receive any letter of apology and then she stated that she had difficulty reading mail. She may have given the mail to her husband and she may have received a letter of apology. I accept that there was some form of apology given to the fourth claimant.

In the port-of-entry notes3 (POE), the SC was asked if he needed food to let the immigration officer know. He replied, "I was told we will get everything for free in Canada." The officer replied, "It doesn't quite work like that. If you are hungry and need food you have money and need to pay for it yourself today." When he was asked if he had made that statement, he said he was tired at the time of the interview and he did not recognize it as his answer. In reply to a further question from his counsel, he stated that he would never say anything like that and that he would not answer it in that manner. He also said that the interpreter was on a telephone when the interview occurred. The immigration officer specifically mentioned this exchange in the notes. I recognize that interviews at the POE are not recorded and to be used with caution, but this was a statement that the officer specifically noted. I find that the SC did make this statement.

The FC stated in his Personal Information Form4 (PIF) narrative that he once had a burning bottle thrown into his living room window and it exploded right inside his home. He says this could have injured any of his children or his wife. In his testimony, he was asked when this incident occurred. He testified that it happened in 1996 or 1997. He stated that the children were in another room and he and his wife were watching television. He states that the police and fire department arrived and a report was made. He was asked if he had requested a copy of the report and he said, "Yes, but the police did not give it to me." It was then pointed out to him that his children were not born in 1996 and 1997. The FC then changed his story and said that he and the second claimant were babysitting his sister's children in her apartment. This is completely different from the story in his PIF and his original testimony. I find that this was a major embellishment to his claim.

The FC also stated in his PIF narrative that three skinheads attacked the second claimant and him on a train to the city of XXXXX in XXXXX 2008. In his testimony, the claimant stated that four or five people attacked the second claimant and him in the town square of XXXXX in 2008. He did not describe any other attack in his initial testimony. It was pointed out to him that he did not mention the attack on train. He then stated that they had been attacked on a train. He was asked why then did he not put the attack in the town square in his PIF narrative. He stated that he did not know why it had not been put in his PIF narrative. If there was an attack in 2008, the FC would have remembered whether it occurred in the town square are on a train. I find that no attack took place in 2008. Discrimination vs. Persecution

Documentary evidence5 states that a number of sources consulted by the Research Directorate indicate that many Roma children in the Czech Republic are sent to special schools that cater to students aged three to nineteen with developmental disabilities. The level of education in special schools has been characterized as substandard and is falling short of providing students with the knowledge necessary for them to enter regular schools. According to the Roma Education Fund, an NGO that seeks to improve the educational opportunities of Roma people, there have been some improvements in Romani education in recent years, including preparatory classes for children from difficult backgrounds to help them make the transition from home to school; teachers' assistants funded by the Ministry of Education who work mainly in schools with high proportion of Roma; free pre-school education in the final year of kindergarten; secondary school scholarships for Roma, which has led to an increase in Romani students in high schools: abolishing special-education schools and thus reducing the social stigma associated with Roma attending institutions for the developmentally disabled; government initiatives and funding have increased, providing a more stable source of funding than irregular private donations.

Various pro-Roma NGOs have developed programs to assist Romani students. The only secondary institution in the Czech Republic specially designed for Romani students, the High School for Social and Legal Issues, has seven branches throughout the country, a total of 600 students, and has graduated 300 students since its inception in 1998. The high school is also the only one to give students classes in Romani language, literature, culture and history. One of the school's teachers notes that the government has had some recent success in integrating greater numbers of Roma into the general education system, "but some teachers still don't want Romani children in their schools. There's still a lot of prejudice. Romani children are still systematically turned away from regular schools and sent to schools where the curriculum is not as challenging and does not meet the minimum requirements for dignity."

There are various reports of high percentages of Romani pupils attending segregated educational institutions however, the Czech government has introduced a "Re-integration of Roma Pupils" project which seeks to correct cases in which Romani students were wrongfully placed in special schools. On November 14, 2007, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in favour of eighteen Romani Czech students who complained of racial discrimination when, following a psychological testing, they had been sent to special schools for children with learning difficulties. The Court found that sending these children to remedial schools amounted to "indirect discrimination" and violated the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court ruled that the Czech government should pay €4000 in costs plus damages to each student. The Court's verdict obliges the Czech Republic and all Council of Europe member states to enact legislation prohibiting discrimination against Romani children in the education system.

In this case the FC, SC, third and fourth claimants testified that they were placed in special schools. The fourth claimant testified that her mother had gone to school to complain about her being transferred to a special school. She states that her mother was charged and was sentenced to a two-year conditional sentence for her actions at the school. There must have been some investigation of the circumstances surrounding this matter. There is no persuasive evidence that this confrontation related to the fourth claimant being sent to a special school. The fifth claimant was placed in a special school but it was acknowledged that he has some mental challenges.

The FC stated in his PIF narrative that his son, the seventh claimant, was put in a special school as soon as he began attending school. It goes on to state that he withdrew his son from school because he lost interest in attending it. In his testimony, he said that he attended school until the family left the Czech Republic. He was asked why there was a difference. He stated that he must have been mistaken. I, again, find that this is an embellishment of his story.

The FC stated that his Roma organization had put a great deal of emphasis on improving the educational opportunities for Roma children. He stated that the high school for Roma children was in the process of being closed because the government had discovered that an American citizen was paying for the school and the owner of the land wanted it back. He described the difficulty for Roma in the educational system. I accept his evidence but I find from the documentary evidence that serious efforts are being made to improve the educational opportunities for Roma children and as outlined above in the documentary evidence, improvements are being made in the actual situation for Roma students. The FC testified that there have been some improvements as a result of the efforts of his Roma organizations.

The placing of the claimants in special schools is obviously a form of discrimination. However, according to the documentary information steps are being taken to deal with this discrimination. In this case, I find that the actions taken in regard to education do not rise to the level of persecution.

The SC was employed until 2005. He was self-employed from 1990 to 2005. He provided employment for other Roma XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. He said that things changed after 2005 when the Czech Republic became part of the European Union. The tax structure changed and machinery replaced human labour. The FC was also employed in the business for a period of time. There were complaints about a Roma individual's record at the employment office being marked with an "R" indicating discrimination in hiring practices. The claimants here were employed for a relatively long period of time either by someone else or through their own business. They may have been some discrimination in hiring practices but in these individual cases there is no persuasive evidence that it rises to the level of persecution.

The FC stated that there had been a petition presented to the non-Roma landlord of the place where they originally lived as a family, complaining about the presence of Roma in the housing units. There is no persuasive evidence that the claimants did not find adequate housing in the Czech Republic.

Does the discrimination suffered by these claimants amount to persecution when considered singularly or cumulatively? To be considered persecution, the mistreatment suffered or anticipated must be serious. In order to determine whether a particular mistreatment would qualify as "serious", one must examine what interest of the claimant might be harmed; and to what extent the subsistence, enjoyment, expression or exercise of that interest might be compromised. "Persecution", for example, undefined in the Convention, has been ascribed the meaning of sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection.6 In the case of Chan,7 La Forest J. (in dissent) reiterated that the essential question is whether the persecution alleged by the claimant threatens his or her basic human rights in a fundamental way.

The physical attacks on the claimants are considered in the following section on state protection. The conclusion reached was that there was no persuasive evidence of a sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights of the claimants demonstrative of a failure of state protection.

I find that these incidents do not rise to the level of persecution when considered individually and I also find that they did not rise to the level of persecution when they are considered cumulatively.

The third and fourth claimants both stated that they had been sterilized without their consent in the Czech Republic. The fourth claimant said that she had gone to the doctor to complain of pain in her abdomen and she was referred to another doctor who performed an operation. She states that she believes she was sterilized as a result. The document8 provided seems to indicate that there is a question as to whether a hysterectomy had been performed. The document also states that there is evidence of a cystic mass in the pelvic area. It is difficult to determine what procedure was performed. There is evidence that a general apology was given by letter but there is a question as to whether the apology related to this specific procedure.

The third claimant stated that she has been sterilized, but the evidence9 presented shows that she has a uterus and both ovaries. She states that she went to the hospital director and the police to complain that she had been sterilized without her consent and that she had commenced a lawsuit. She subsequently changed her testimony to say that there had been no lawsuit. There is obviously concern about the alleged procedures but there is no persuasive evidence that any operation was done without consent.

Documentary evidence10 states that the government continued to investigate cases of forced sterilization, mainly of Romani women, since the 1970's. According to a 2005 report by the ombudsman, most allegations of forced sterilization date to the 1973-1991 period. However, the non-governmental organization (NGO) Group of Women Harmed by Sterilization (WHS) reported that its field research uncovered two recent cases, one in November 2008, the other in 2007. In the latter case WHS was seeking legal representation for the victim. The Ostrava Regional Court ruled in October that a local hospital was liable for the wrongful sterilization performed on a Romani woman, 11 years prior and awarded her 50,000 koruna ($2,600) and an apology. The hospital appealed and the appeal court ruled that she was not entitled to financial damages because the deadline for making such claims had passed but upheld the requirement that the hospital apologize. The woman appealed this decision to the Supreme Court in Brno. The case was pending at year's end.

In 2007, the government Council for Human Rights proposed to pay each sterilization victim 200,000 korunas ($10,400) in compensation but the government rejected the proposal. At year's end the government was seeking assistance from the Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes to establish the extent to which sterilizations before 1989 were government policy and to what extent individual hospital and social workers were responsible.
If the operations were performed on these women without their consent then it appears there were some avenues of redress which could be pursued.

I have considered the psychological assessment of XXXXX XXXXX 11 in regard to the fourth claimant. I accept it for the purpose of assessing the subjective fear of the claimant. The fourth claimant was questioned first by her counsel as a result of the report. State Protection

I also considered the issue of state protection. In assessing the issue, I am guided by a number of cases. The principles were applied to this case. There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens. A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the evidence establishes that the state protection is inadequate.12 A claimant can rebut the presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. For example, a claimant might advance testimony of similarly situated individuals let down by the state protection arrangement or the claimant's testimony of past personal incidents in which state protection did not materialize. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming 13 While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration,14 recent Federal Court decisions have held that the test for a finding of state protection is whether the protection is adequate, rather than the effectiveness per se.15 16 17 18 19 20 21 The protection need not be perfect.22 One accepted measure of assessment is whether the state is making "serious efforts" to protect its citizens.23 This standard continues to be applied in many Federal Court decisions.24 25 26 27

As stated above, no government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state, in not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.28 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.29

Furthermore, the law states that the burden to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.30 The Czech Republic is a democracy with free and fair elections.31 Therefore, the presumption of state protection is a strong one. The claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.32 Moreover, local failures by the authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state, as a whole, fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.33 Indeed, if a claimant believes the actions of some police officers are corrupt, the onus is on them to approach other members of the security forces or authorities.34 There is nothing in the documentation before the Board to suggest that the Czech Republic is in a state of complete breakdown.

The Czech Republic generally respected and protected the rights of its citizens.35 There is legislation in place that provides state protection for the Roma: including anti-discrimination and hate crime legislation.36 The Czech constitution prohibits discrimination based on national, racial or ethnic background as well as other pieces of legislation governing employment and education as well as The Charter of Rights and Freedoms.37 An anti-discrimination bill, which would harmonize Czech legislation with that of the European Union, was passed on June 17, 2009. Furthermore, the Czech Republic is a member of the European Union, which has had a positive impact on the country by setting standards concerning human rights, as well as access to the European Court of Human Rights and access to multilateral programs such as The Decade of Roma Inclusion.38

In order to address acts of discrimination the Czech Republic government introduced the Roma Police Assistants (RPA's).39 The purpose of employing RPA's is his to assist in building better relations and trust between the Roma and the police. The RPA's assist police in their investigations, assist in accompanying Romani who are victims of crime to file police reports and help obtain social services for such victims. It has been found that the RPA's and other minority liaison officers have been effective in helping the Roma. Furthermore, in the mid-1990s, the Ministry of the Interior (who is responsible for maintaining the national police force in the Czech Republic) initiated programs to combat extremism (including the neo-Nazis) by allowing the police to closely monitor such group activities and it is showing signs of success.40 The police have arrested neo-Nazis and they have been prosecuted, including a case where a Romani had been murdered. The police successfully prevented a clash of neo-Nazis in Bruno and expelled them from the city.41 The government is also trying to recruit Roma as police officers, with the number of drives being conducted in Prague and Brno. If a Romani is interested in becoming a police officer but lacks the formal education requirement, the police offer assistance for that person to complete any education requirement so that they can then join the police force.42 Furthermore, the police are trained on how to deal with minorities.43 The police are making other efforts such as participating in day camps, seminars and school visits in order to foster better relations with the Roma.44 As of 2006, there were an estimated 61 Romani police officers in the Czech Republic.45

The judiciary has prosecuted hate crimes committed against the Roma on several occasions. The Issue Paper notes that judicial proceedings on racial crime have increased in recent years due to the efforts of NGO's. The Czech Ombudsman, created in 1999 and is known as the Public Defender of Human Rights, investigates allegations of public-sector mistreatment of Roma and takes corrective actions to remedy such situations.46 There are other government and non government agencies available to assist the Roma, including 400 Romani NGOs, the Czech Trade Inspectorate (to deal with unfair business practices or consumer discrimination), the Czech Helsinki Committee to investigate cases of police misconduct involving the Roma And the Social Inclusion and Agency to ad in dress the social integration of the Roma into Czech society, including housing, healthcare, employment, social services and cohesion.47 The preponderance of the documentary evidence indicates that the Czech Republic government is making very serious efforts to provide protection to the Roma whether as victims of hate crime, assist in obtaining health care or education or inclusion into Czech society. As noted above, there is discrimination against the Roma in various aspects of their lives. However the Czech government is making very serious efforts to overcome this discrimination.

The SC stated that as resulted of the assault suffered by him and other members of his organization n Prague in 1990, that the individual by the name of XXXXX was held in custody for a period of six months, apparently without charge, while the matter was investigated. The SC testified that XXXXX was compensated in the amount of 42,000 Czech korunas as result of this matter. The police had obviously investigated the situation and determined that a mistake was made and paid compensation. The SC says that he was attacked on two other occasions in 2002 and 2003. He says that he went to the police report these incidents and he returned to check on the matters but he never heard any results of the investigation. He states that he could not provide any police reports because he was told that the police did not keep records for more than five years. There is no persuasive evidence that the police did not investigate these matters.

As outlined above, I do not accept the credibility of the FC in his statements of alleged attacks. In addition, the FC stated that he had been mistreated when he received a sentence of four months imprisonment for theft of a Digital Versatile Disc (it once stood for Digital Video Disc) (DVD) player. He says he participated at the instigation of some non-Roma individuals but he admitted that the police found him in possession of the DVD player. There is no persuasive evidence that the sentence he received was overly harsh because of his Roma ethnicity. He testified that a state appointed counsel represented him at the hearing and he pleaded guilty to the charge.

The attack on the fifth claimant in 2008 was vicious according to the report48 entered as evidence. The attack occurred on XXXXX, 2008 and the claimants left the Czech Republic on XXXXX, 2008. This was only two months after the attack. This was a short period of time for the police to investigate the matter.

The FC stated that a male cousin of the third claimant, his wife, had been employed by the police in the regional office of the area where they lived. He states that one day when he arrived at the police station he found his locker had been ransacked and there were writings telling him to leave the police force. He says that he did leave the police forces result of this and his organization became involved in the matter but they were unable to solve it satisfactorily. The FC was asked if this person had taken any other action as a result of what happened. The FC replied that he did not know because he had left the country.
I find that there is no persuasive evidence of a sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights of the claimants demonstrative of a failure of state protection.

In the cases where a claimant reported a matter the police appeared to have responded. The claimants may not have been satisfied with the results but I find that they have not rebutted the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

Having considered all of the evidence, I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, rejects the claims for refugee protection.
